**[II. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY]{.underline}**

Based on the analysis set forth in detail in Parts III and IV of this memorandum, our principal findings and recommendations are summarized as follows.

**Royalty Rate Benchmarking.** Our review of comparable premium lifestyle and boutique hotel brand license transactions --- encompassing fourteen identified comparable transactions executed between 2019 and 2024 --- indicates that a royalty rate of 4.0% of Net Room Revenue is at or slightly below the market median for licenses of this profile. The median observed royalty rate across the comparable data set is approximately 4.1% of Net Room Revenue, with a mean of approximately 4.15%. A royalty rate of 3.25% of Net Room Revenue, as proposed by Peregrine, falls below the 25th percentile of observed comparable rates (approximately 3.65%) and places the proposed transaction in the bottom decile of the data set when adjusted for portfolio size and brand strength. The policy-floor rate of 4.0% established by Licensing Policy § 5.2(a) is therefore consistent with, and indeed modestly below, prevailing market rates for transactions of comparable scope and brand positioning.

**Enforcement Risk.** Peregrine\'s proposed modifications to the quality control provisions of the TLA raise material enforcement risks under the Lanham Act. Specifically, Peregrine has proposed: (i) reducing on-site audit frequency from semi-annual to annual, with an increase in the notice period from five business days to twenty business days; (ii) introducing a deemed-approval mechanism under which licensor non-response within fifteen business days constitutes automatic approval of licensee quality control submissions; and (iii) permitting affiliate sublicensing to Peregrine-controlled affiliates without prior written Veltris consent. Individually, each of these proposals weakens Veltris\'s ability to demonstrate the exercise of adequate quality control over the use of the AURANOVA Marks. Collectively, these proposals create material risks of naked licensing exposure, trademark dilution, and potential loss of rights under Lanham Act § 45 (15 U.S.C. § 1127). The combined adoption of all three proposals would produce an enforcement posture that falls below the threshold of \"adequate quality control\" as interpreted by the Seventh and Ninth Circuits, among other federal courts.

**Overall Recommendation.** The proposed deviations from Licensing Policy §§ 5.2 through 5.8 warrant careful scrutiny, and Whitfield Barr recommends that any concessions in these areas be accompanied by robust contractual safeguards as described in Part IV of this memorandum. In particular, we recommend that deemed-approval clauses be rejected entirely, that audit frequency remain semi-annual at minimum, and that any flexibility on affiliate sublicensing be conditioned upon the specific protective mechanisms described in Section IV.D below.

**[III. BRAND VALUATION BENCHMARKING --- ROYALTY RATE ANALYSIS]{.underline}**

**A. Methodology.** In conducting the royalty rate benchmarking analysis, Whitfield Barr employed a multi-source analytical methodology designed to identify and evaluate a representative set of comparable trademark license transactions in the premium lifestyle and boutique hospitality sector. The analysis drew upon the following sources:

**Publicly available and proprietary licensing transaction databases.** We reviewed transaction data compiled by RoyaltyStat LLC, ktMINE, and the Licensing Economics Review database, filtering for trademark license agreements in the hospitality and lodging sector with disclosed royalty rate terms. These databases aggregate publicly filed and voluntarily reported licensing transactions and provide a starting point for identifying comparable rate structures.

**SEC filings disclosing trademark license terms.** We reviewed annual reports (Form 10-K), quarterly reports (Form 10-Q), and current reports (Form 8-K) filed by publicly traded hospitality companies with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission for the period 2019 through 2024. In several instances, these filings disclosed the material terms of trademark license agreements --- including royalty rates, minimum annual guarantees, and quality control provisions --- in connection with related-party transactions, material definitive agreements, or risk factor disclosures. While the level of disclosure varies among filers, the SEC filing data provided useful corroboration of rates observed in the proprietary databases.

**Industry surveys and publications.** We reviewed industry surveys and reports published by the American Hotel & Lodging Association, the Boutique & Lifestyle Leaders Association, the Licensing Industry Merchandisers\' Association, and several IP valuation advisory firms, including Consor Intellectual Asset Management and Intangible Business Ltd. These publications provide aggregate market data on royalty rate ranges by industry segment and brand tier.

**Whitfield Barr\'s own transaction experience.** Our firm has advised on trademark licensing transactions in the hospitality sector for over fifteen years, and we drew upon our experience in structuring and negotiating comparable agreements to contextualize the data set and assess the relevance of individual comparables.

The universe of comparable transactions was defined as follows: trademark license agreements for premium lifestyle, boutique, and upper-upscale hotel brands in the United States, involving a net room revenue royalty structure, executed between January 1, 2019 and December 31, 2024. To ensure relevance to the AURANOVA transaction, we applied the following key selection parameters:

> \(a\) **Brand positioning.** The licensed brand must be positioned in the premium boutique, lifestyle, or upper-upscale segment of the U.S. lodging market, consistent with the market positioning of the AURANOVA brand.
>
> \(b\) **Licensor-licensee structure.** The transaction must involve a brand owner (licensor) licensing its trademarks to a hotel operator and/or developer (licensee), rather than a management contract or joint venture with equity participation by the brand owner.
>
> \(c\) **Royalty base.** The royalty must be calculated as a percentage of net room revenue, which is the predominant royalty structure in the premium lifestyle/boutique hotel licensing sector and the structure contemplated in the Peregrine TLA.
>
> \(d\) **Portfolio size.** The license must cover a portfolio of approximately eight to twenty properties, consistent with the twelve-property scope of the Peregrine transaction. Single-property licenses were excluded as not comparable in terms of scale economics and brand deployment scope.
>
> \(e\) **Geographic scope.** The license must be limited to defined regions within the United States, consistent with the geographic scope of the Peregrine TLA, which covers the Southeastern United States.

The following categories of transactions were excluded from the comparable data set as structurally distinct from the AURANOVA--Peregrine negotiation:

> \(i\) Franchise agreements structured under the FTC Franchise Rule (16 C.F.R. Part 436), which involve regulatory disclosure obligations, franchise fees, and ongoing operational mandates that are materially different from trademark-only licenses.
>
> \(ii\) Management company arrangements with equity participation by the brand owner, which reflect a fundamentally different risk-<REDACTED> model and typically involve revenue-sharing structures rather than royalty-based compensation.
>
> \(iii\) International cross-border licenses, which involve currency risk, jurisdictional differences in trademark law, and market-specific pricing considerations that render them incomparable to domestic U.S. transactions.

Applying these criteria, we identified fourteen comparable transactions that form the basis of the quantitative analysis set forth below. Three representative transactions are described in detail in Section III.B; the remaining eleven transactions were reviewed and their terms are reflected in the aggregate statistical analysis presented in Section III.C.

The appropriate mechanism for addressing Peregrine\'s rebranding investment is a structural accommodation --- such as a phased MAG ramp-up or a CapEx co-investment provision --- rather than a permanent reduction in the ongoing royalty rate.

**The upfront license fee does not offset the annual royalty shortfall.** Peregrine\'s proposed upfront license fee of \$750,000 meets the Licensing Policy minimum of \$500,000 and exceeds it by \$250,000. Over the proposed ten-year initial term, the cumulative royalty shortfall would exceed \$5,850,000 (assuming flat revenue), a figure that dwarfs the \$250,000 increment in the upfront license fee above the policy minimum. **[IV. ENFORCEMENT RISK ANALYSIS]{.underline}**

**A. Analytical Framework**

In addition to the royalty rate issues addressed above, this memorandum analyzes enforcement risks arising from three specific proposals advanced by Peregrine in the ongoing TLA negotiations. The proposals at issue are:

> \(1\) **Reduced Audit Frequency.** Peregrine proposes to reduce on-site quality audit frequency from semi-annual to annual and to increase the required advance notice period from five business days to twenty business days.
>
> \(2\) **Deemed-Approval Mechanism.** Peregrine proposes to introduce a deemed-approval provision under which licensor non-response to licensee quality submissions within fifteen business days constitutes automatic approval of the submitted materials, including brand usage applications, marketing collateral, and quality control reports.
>
> \(3\) **Affiliate Sublicensing Without Prior Consent.** Peregrine proposes to sublicense the AURANOVA Marks to Peregrine-controlled affiliates without obtaining prior written Veltris consent, subject only to a post-hoc notification requirement within thirty calendar days of the sublicense execution.

The analysis that follows is framed under the Lanham Act\'s requirement that a trademark licensor must exercise adequate quality control over its licensee\'s use of the licensed marks. This requirement is rooted in the fundamental trademark principle that a mark serves as an indicator of source and that the consuming public relies on the mark as a guarantor of consistent quality. When a licensor fails to exercise meaningful quality control over its licensee\'s use of the mark, the resulting \"naked license\" may constitute abandonment of the mark under 15 U.S.C. § 1127 (Lanham Act § 45). The statute provides that a mark is deemed abandoned when \"any course of conduct of the owner, including acts of omission as well as commission, causes the mark to \... lose its significance as a mark.\"

The Veltris IP Licensing Policy directly addresses these risks. Sections 5.3 (audit frequency and quality control standards), 5.3(c) (approval mechanisms), and 5.6 (sublicensing) establish baseline safeguards that are consistent with, and in many respects more protective than, the minimum requirements imposed by the Lanham Act. These provisions were adopted following a comprehensive review of trademark enforcement best practices conducted in 2023, and they reflect Veltris\'s considered judgment --- supported by outside counsel advice --- regarding the level of quality control necessary to maintain the enforceability and value of its trademark portfolio.

It bears emphasis that the AURANOVA Marks (U.S. Trademark Reg. Nos. 5,417,832; 5,822,109; and 6,004,561) represent significant brand equity developed over more than a decade of investment in marketing, guest experience development, and brand standards cultivation. Loss of or impairment to any of these registrations would have consequences far beyond the Peregrine transaction, potentially affecting Veltris\'s ability to enforce the AURANOVA brand across all existing and prospective licensing relationships, product line extensions, and co-branded ventures.

**B. Reduced Audit Frequency**

Peregrine has proposed reducing on-site quality audits from a semi-annual schedule with five business days\' advance notice to an annual schedule with twenty business days\' advance notice. This proposal was first communicated during the February 6, 2025 negotiation session and was reiterated in Peregrine\'s March 3, 2025 markup of the quality control provisions. Whitfield Barr has analyzed this proposal and concludes that it materially weakens Veltris\'s quality control posture and the evidentiary record supporting Veltris\'s ongoing exercise of adequate oversight.

**Dual Function of Semi-Annual Audits.** Semi-annual on-site quality audits serve a dual function in the context of a trademark license agreement. First, they provide a mechanism for verifying the licensee\'s ongoing compliance with the licensor\'s quality standards and brand guidelines. This is the operational function: semi-annual audits enable the licensor to identify deviations from brand standards --- including deficiencies in guest experience, physical plant maintenance, signage and collateral compliance, and service delivery --- in a timely manner, before such deviations become entrenched or visible to consumers. Second, and equally important, semi-annual audits create a documented record that the licensor is exercising meaningful supervisory control over the licensee\'s use of the marks. This is the evidentiary function: in any future proceeding in which the adequacy of Veltris\'s quality control is challenged --- whether in a cancellation proceeding, an infringement defense, or a dilution claim --- the frequency, regularity, and rigor of the audit record will be a central element of Veltris\'s defense.

**Risks of Annual Audit Frequency.** Moving to an annual audit schedule doubles the window during which quality deviations could go undetected. In the context of a twelve-property rebranding --- particularly during the critical first twelve to eighteen months of the launch, when consumer impressions of the AURANOVA brand are being formed at each new Peregrine property --- a full year between on-site inspections is a significant gap. Guest reviews, online brand perception, and word-of-mouth referrals are formed in the earliest months of a property\'s operation under a new brand. Quality deficiencies that persist for twelve months before detection can cause lasting damage to consumer associations with the AURANOVA name, damage that may be difficult or impossible to remediate even after the deficiency is corrected. Furthermore, an annual audit cadence provides limited opportunity for iterative feedback and course-correction during the ramp-up period, when the licensee\'s operational teams are most likely to be adjusting to new brand standards.

**Risks of Extended Notice Period.** Peregrine\'s proposal to increase the notice period from five business days to twenty business days compounds the audit frequency concern. A twenty-business-day notice requirement effectively provides Peregrine approximately one calendar month of advance warning before any on-site inspection. This extended notice period creates the opportunity for temporary remediation of persistent issues --- a well-known phenomenon in the quality assurance field sometimes referred to as \"audit preparation\" --- in which a property is brought into superficial compliance for the duration of an inspection but reverts to non-compliant conditions thereafter. A shorter notice period, by contrast, increases the likelihood that the audit will capture the property\'s ordinary operating conditions and provide an accurate assessment of ongoing brand standards compliance.

**Comparison to Comparable Transactions.** The audit provisions in the three representative comparable transactions described in Part III are instructive. Comparable Transaction No. 1 provided for semi-annual on-site audits with ten business days\' notice. Comparable Transaction No. 2 provided for quarterly quality control inspections with seven business days\' notice. Comparable Transaction No. 3 provided for monthly quality reporting supplemented by semi-annual on-site inspections. None of the three representative comparables --- and, more broadly, none of the fourteen transactions in the full data set --- provided for annual-only audits, and none included a notice period exceeding ten business days. Peregrine\'s proposed annual audit with twenty business days\' notice is an outlier in the market and is inconsistent with prevailing practice among licensors of comparable premium brands.

**Legal Assessment.** While reduced audit frequency alone may not, in isolation, constitute naked licensing sufficient to support a finding of abandonment, it materially weakens the evidentiary record that Veltris could present to defend the AURANOVA registrations if challenged on quality control grounds. Courts evaluating naked licensing claims look to the totality of the licensor\'s quality control efforts, and a shift from semi-annual to annual audits would be viewed as a significant reduction in oversight --- particularly when combined with the other modifications proposed by Peregrine, as discussed in Sections IV.C and IV.D below.

**C. Deemed-Approval Clauses**

Peregrine has proposed a deemed-approval mechanism under which quality control submissions, brand usage approvals, and marketing materials submitted by the licensee are automatically deemed approved if Veltris does not respond within fifteen business days of submission. This provision would apply to all categories of licensee submissions requiring licensor approval, including property-level brand compliance reports, proposed signage and collateral designs, digital and print marketing materials, and guest-facing service standards documentation.

**Structural Risk of Passive Approval.** Deemed-approval mechanisms create a structural risk that non-conforming uses of the AURANOVA Marks will receive automatic approval through licensor inaction. In the ordinary course of a multi-property licensing relationship, the volume of submissions requiring licensor review can be substantial. Staff transitions, competing priorities, internal review bottlenecks, and simple administrative delay --- none of which reflect a deliberate decision to approve a submission --- can result in the expiration of a fifteen-business-day review window. Under Peregrine\'s proposal, such expiration would constitute affirmative approval of the submitted materials, regardless of whether any Veltris representative had actually reviewed them. This means that non-conforming signage, off-brand marketing collateral, or substandard quality reports could receive \"approval\" without any human review by Veltris\'s brand assurance team. The result is a systematic undermining of the quality control function that the approval requirement is designed to serve.

**Judicial Treatment of Quality Control Failures.** Federal courts have consistently held that a trademark licensor must do more than retain the contractual right to control quality --- it must actually exercise that right. Two decisions are particularly instructive in the context of Peregrine\'s deemed-approval proposal.

In *Eva\'s Bridal Ltd. v. Halanick Enterprises, Inc.*, 639 F.3d 788 (7th Cir. 2011), the Seventh Circuit addressed the question of what constitutes adequate quality control in the context of a trademark license. The court held that the licensor\'s failure to exercise meaningful control over the quality of goods sold under its mark constituted naked licensing and resulted in abandonment. The court\'s analysis focused on whether the licensor had both retained and exercised the contractual right to inspect and control quality. Critically, the court distinguished between the mere existence of quality control provisions in a license agreement and the licensor\'s actual exercise of those provisions. A deemed-approval mechanism is directly relevant to this distinction: it converts licensor inaction into affirmative consent, thereby creating a contractual structure in which the licensor can \"exercise\" quality control by doing nothing. This is precisely the type of passive oversight that the *Eva\'s Bridal* court found insufficient to maintain trademark rights. The court emphasized that a licensor must take affirmative steps to monitor and enforce quality standards, and a deemed-approval clause is antithetical to that requirement.

In *Barcamerica International USA Trust v. Tyfield Importers, Inc.*, 289 F.3d 589 (9th Cir. 2002), the Ninth Circuit addressed a similar question and reached a similar conclusion. The licensor in *Barcamerica* argued that it had relied on the licensee\'s own quality control processes to ensure consistent quality, without conducting independent verification. The Ninth Circuit rejected this argument, holding that \"a licensor must take some reasonable steps to monitor and control the quality of the products bearing its mark\" and that mere \"reliance on a licensee\'s own quality control\" is insufficient. The court specifically held that the licensor must \"retain\[\] and exercise\[\] adequate control\" over the nature and quality of the goods or services offered under the mark. The *Barcamerica* court found naked licensing where the licensor had essentially delegated all quality assurance to the licensee without independent oversight --- a scenario that bears a direct analogy to a deemed-approval provision, which similarly delegates the final approval decision to the passage of time rather than to the licensor\'s affirmative judgment.

**Application to Peregrine\'s Proposal.** The connection between the *Eva\'s Bridal* and *Barcamerica* holdings and Peregrine\'s deemed-approval proposal is direct and compelling. A clause that converts fifteen business days of licensor silence into automatic approval is functionally equivalent to the passive, assumption-based oversight that both courts found insufficient to support a finding of adequate quality control. Under such a provision, Veltris would not be required to affirmatively evaluate and approve each submission; instead, the mere passage of time would serve as a proxy for the licensor\'s exercise of judgment. This is the antithesis of the \"meaningful control\" that the Lanham Act requires.

Moreover, the deemed-approval mechanism would be a permanent feature of the TLA --- not a one-time accommodation --- meaning that every quality submission over the life of the agreement would be subject to automatic approval in the event of any delay in Veltris\'s response. Over a ten-year term covering twelve properties, the cumulative volume of submissions that could receive deemed approval without actual licensor review is substantial, creating an extensive record of passive oversight that could be cited by any party seeking to challenge Veltris\'s quality control practices.

**Policy Prohibition.** Deemed-approval provisions are expressly prohibited under Veltris IP Licensing Policy § 5.3(c), which provides that \"\[n\]o license agreement shall include any \'deemed approval,\' \'deemed consent,\' or \'deemed acceptance\' mechanism of any kind\" and states that this prohibition \"is absolute.\" This prohibition reflects not merely an internal policy preference but a legally grounded strategy to preserve the enforceability of the AURANOVA registrations. The prohibition was adopted upon the recommendation of outside trademark counsel following the *Eva\'s Bridal* and *Barcamerica* decisions and is consistent with the guidance published by the International Trademark Association regarding best practices for trademark licensing quality control.

**Conclusion.** Inclusion of a deemed-approval clause in the TLA would expose Veltris to a colorable argument --- in any future infringement action, cancellation proceeding, or opposition proceeding --- that the AURANOVA Marks have been subject to naked licensing. Even if a court were to conclude that the deemed-approval provision alone did not rise to the level of abandonment, the provision would constitute a significant piece of adverse evidence that could be weighed alongside other quality control deficiencies. The risk is not merely theoretical; it is a litigation risk that Veltris would carry for the duration of the license term and beyond.

**D. Affiliate Sublicensing Without Prior Consent**

Peregrine has proposed that it be permitted to sublicense the AURANOVA Marks to its controlled affiliates --- defined in Peregrine\'s draft as entities in which Peregrine Hospitality Group, LLC holds, directly or indirectly, a majority ownership interest --- without obtaining prior written Veltris consent. Under the proposal, Peregrine would be required only to provide written notice to Veltris within thirty calendar days of executing any such affiliate sublicense. Whitfield Barr has analyzed this proposal and concludes that it poses significant quality control, dilution, and abandonment risks.

**Scope of Potential Expansion.** Peregrine currently operates thirty-four boutique hotel properties across the Southeastern United States through a network of affiliated operating entities. The current transaction covers twelve of these properties, which are to be rebranded under the \"AURANOVA by Peregrine\" co-branded concept. Peregrine\'s affiliate sublicensing proposal would permit any Peregrine-controlled affiliate to use the AURANOVA Marks at additional properties beyond the twelve that have been specifically evaluated, negotiated, and approved by Veltris. In effect, the proposal would allow the scope of AURANOVA brand deployment to expand from twelve properties to as many as thirty-four (or more, as Peregrine acquires or develops additional properties) without any advance review or consent by Veltris. The significance of this expansion cannot be overstated: Veltris would be permitting the use of the AURANOVA Marks at properties it has never inspected, by operators it has never evaluated, and under conditions it has never approved.

**Quality Control Implications.** Each affiliate sublicensee operates independently at the property level, with its own management team, service staff, physical plant, and operational practices. The quality of the guest experience, the condition of the physical facilities, the execution of the brand standards, and the use of the AURANOVA Marks in signage, marketing, and digital media vary from property to property and from operator to operator. Veltris\'s ability to maintain the consistent quality that the AURANOVA brand represents to consumers depends on its ability to evaluate each property and each operator before the marks are deployed. Affiliate sublicensing without prior consent eliminates this critical gatekeeping function. By the time Veltris receives notice of an affiliate sublicense --- up to thirty days after execution --- the AURANOVA Marks may already be in use at a property that does not meet AURANOVA brand standards.

**Trademark Dilution Risk.** Under the Federal Trademark Dilution Revision Act (15 U.S.C. § 1125(c)), dilution by blurring occurs when the use of a mark similar or identical to a famous or distinctive mark weakens the distinctiveness of that mark by creating associations with products or services of varying quality. While the AURANOVA Marks would be used by Peregrine affiliates in the same hospitality sector, the risk of dilution by blurring arises from the inconsistency of quality across affiliate properties. If some affiliate sublicensees operate properties that fall below AURANOVA brand standards --- whether due to deferred maintenance, undertrained staff, or inadequate service delivery --- the resulting consumer experience will dilute the distinctive quality associations that the AURANOVA brand has cultivated. Consumers who encounter a substandard \"AURANOVA by Peregrine\" experience at an affiliate property will form negative associations that attach to the AURANOVA brand as a whole, weakening its distinctiveness and reducing its value across all licensing relationships and product categories.

**Abandonment Risk Under Lanham Act § 45.** As noted above, the Lanham Act provides that a mark is deemed abandoned when \"any course of conduct of the owner, including acts of omission as well as commission,\" causes the mark to lose its significance as a mark. Permitting sublicensing without consent is an act of omission in the exercise of quality control: it represents a deliberate decision by the licensor to forgo its opportunity to evaluate and approve each sublicensee before the marks are deployed. Courts evaluating abandonment claims look to whether the licensor has taken affirmative steps to monitor and control the use of its marks by sublicensees, and a blanket authorization for affiliate sublicensing without consent provides strong evidence that the licensor has abdicated its quality control obligations.

**Compounding Effect.** The affiliate sublicensing proposal does not exist in isolation. When considered in combination with the reduced audit frequency and deemed-approval provisions also proposed by Peregrine, the cumulative effect is a near-complete abdication of quality control over sublicensee use of the AURANOVA Marks. Under the combined proposals, the following scenario becomes possible: Peregrine sublicenses the AURANOVA Marks to an affiliate operating a property that Veltris has never inspected; the affiliate submits quality control materials that are deemed approved because Veltris does not respond within fifteen business days; and Veltris does not conduct an on-site audit of the affiliate\'s property for up to twelve months, after receiving twenty business days\' notice that provides ample time for temporary remediation. In this scenario, a Peregrine affiliate could operate under the AURANOVA Marks for a year or more with effectively zero meaningful quality oversight by Veltris. The synergistic interaction of these three proposals creates an enforcement posture that would be difficult to defend in any legal proceeding challenging the adequacy of Veltris\'s quality control.

**Policy Requirement.** Veltris IP Licensing Policy § 5.6(a) provides that the licensee shall not sublicense any right to use the Licensed IP \"without the prior written consent of Veltris, which Veltris may withhold in its sole and absolute discretion,\" and that this requirement \"applies to all proposed sublicenses regardless of the relationship between the licensee and the proposed sublicensee, including sublicenses to Controlled Affiliates.\" The policy further prohibits any \"automatic, pre-approved, or blanket sublicensing right\" for affiliates or related entities. This provision admits of no exceptions and reflects Veltris\'s considered judgment that the quality control risks associated with uncontrolled sublicensing --- even to affiliated entities --- are too significant to permit blanket authorizations.

**Recommended Safeguards.** If, notwithstanding the foregoing analysis, the Veltris IP Licensing team and Brand Governance Committee determine that some degree of flexibility on affiliate sublicensing is warranted as a negotiating concession, Whitfield Barr recommends that any such flexibility be conditioned upon the following minimum safeguards:

> \(i\) **Advance Identification.** Peregrine must identify each proposed affiliate sublicensee in advance, providing Veltris with the affiliate\'s legal name, organizational structure, ownership, property portfolio, and a description of the property or properties at which the AURANOVA Marks would be used.
>
> \(ii\) **Direct Quality Control Undertaking.** Each affiliate sublicensee must execute a direct quality control undertaking in favor of Veltris, in a form approved by Veltris, under which the sublicensee acknowledges Veltris\'s ownership of the AURANOVA Marks, agrees to comply with the AURANOVA Brand Standards Manual (as amended from time to time), and submits to Veltris\'s quality control and audit rights.
>
> \(iii\) **Independent Audit Rights.** Veltris must retain the right to conduct independent on-site audits of each affiliate sublicensee\'s property on the same schedule and under the same notice provisions as those applicable to the primary licensee. No reduction in audit frequency or increase in notice periods for sublicensee properties shall be permitted.
>
> \(iv\) **Immediate Cessation Right.** Veltris must retain the right to require immediate cessation of any affiliate sublicensee\'s use of the AURANOVA Marks upon a determination by Veltris that the sublicensee has failed to meet AURANOVA brand standards, without being required to first pursue cure or remediation procedures.

These safeguards are designed to preserve Veltris\'s ability to exercise meaningful quality control over each sublicensee\'s use of the AURANOVA Marks, while providing Peregrine with the operational flexibility to deploy the AURANOVA brand across its affiliate network subject to appropriate oversight.

**E. Cumulative Risk Assessment and Loss-of-Rights Scenarios**

The individual risk analyses set forth in Sections IV.B through IV.D above are concerning on their own terms. However, the most significant risk arises from the cumulative effect of adopting all three of Peregrine\'s proposed modifications. Taken together, annual audits with extended notice, deemed-approval mechanisms, and uncontrolled affiliate sublicensing would create an enforcement posture that falls below the threshold of \"adequate quality control\" as interpreted by federal courts. The combination produces a licensing arrangement in which Veltris retains nominal quality control rights but lacks the practical mechanisms to exercise those rights in any meaningful way. This is precisely the scenario that the naked licensing doctrine is designed to address.

The specific loss-of-rights scenarios that could result from the combined adoption of these proposals are as follows:

**Scenario 1: Cancellation Proceeding.** A third party --- whether a competitor, a disgruntled consumer, or a prospective licensee --- could initiate a cancellation proceeding before the Trademark Trial and Appeal Board (\"TTAB\") seeking to cancel one or more of the AURANOVA registrations (Reg. Nos. 5,417,832; 5,822,109; and 6,004,561) on the ground of abandonment through naked licensing. In such a proceeding, the petitioner could introduce the Peregrine TLA as Exhibit A --- a license agreement under which the trademark owner has authorized annual-only audits with month-long notice periods, deemed-approval of quality submissions, and affiliate sublicensing without consent. The TTAB would evaluate whether these provisions, individually and collectively, demonstrate that Veltris has failed to exercise adequate quality control over the use of its marks. The risk of an adverse finding is substantial.

**Scenario 2: Infringement Defense.** In any trademark infringement action brought by Veltris under 15 U.S.C. § 1114 or § 1125(a), a defendant could assert as an affirmative defense that Veltris has abandoned the AURANOVA Marks through naked licensing. The defendant would argue that Veltris\'s own licensing practices --- as evidenced by the Peregrine TLA --- demonstrate that the AURANOVA Marks no longer serve as reliable indicators of source because Veltris has abdicated its quality control responsibilities. The deemed-approval and affiliate sublicensing provisions would be cited as evidence that Veltris has delegated quality control to its licensees and their affiliates without meaningful oversight. If the court were to credit this defense, Veltris\'s infringement claim would fail, and the court\'s finding of abandonment could have preclusive effect in subsequent proceedings.

**Scenario 3: Dilution Claim Weakened.** If Veltris seeks to assert dilution claims under 15 U.S.C. § 1125(c), the existence of inadequately controlled sublicenses undermines the argument that the AURANOVA Marks retain the strong, distinctive source-identifying significance necessary to support a dilution claim. A court evaluating dilution by blurring would consider, among other factors, the distinctiveness of the mark and the extent to which the owner has taken steps to preserve that distinctiveness. Evidence that the mark is being used by unvetted affiliate sublicensees under a deemed-approval regime with infrequent audits would weigh against a finding of strong distinctiveness and could be fatal to a dilution claim.

**Stakes Beyond the Peregrine Transaction.** The AURANOVA brand is not limited to the Peregrine relationship. The AURANOVA Marks are used across multiple licensing relationships, product categories, and co-branded ventures that collectively generate significant annual revenue for Veltris. Loss of or impairment to the federal registrations would have cascading consequences extending well beyond the Peregrine transaction. Other licensees could seek to renegotiate their license terms on the ground that the marks have been weakened. Prospective licensees could demand reduced royalty rates reflecting the diminished enforceability of the registrations. Competitors could adopt confusingly similar marks with reduced fear of enforcement. The reputational damage to the Veltris IP portfolio as a whole could be substantial and long-lasting.

The enforcement risks identified in this Part IV are not hypothetical. They are grounded in established case law, recognized by the leading trademark treatises, and constitute precisely the kind of risk that the Veltris IP Licensing Policy §§ 5.4 through 5.8 were specifically designed to mitigate. The Policy\'s quality control requirements exist not as arbitrary constraints on deal flexibility but as legally necessary safeguards for the preservation of Veltris\'s trademark rights. Deviations from these requirements should be granted only in exceptional circumstances and only with the robust contractual protections necessary to mitigate the resulting enforcement exposure.

**[V. SUMMARY OF FINDINGS AND RECOMMENDATIONS]{.underline}**

**A. Royalty Rate**

Based on the benchmarking analysis set forth in Part III of this memorandum, Whitfield Barr concludes that the Veltris IP Licensing Policy floor rate of 4.0% of Net Room Revenue is at or slightly below the market median for premium lifestyle and boutique hotel brand trademark licenses. The comparable transaction data set supports a median rate of approximately 4.1% and a 25th percentile rate of approximately 3.65%. Peregrine\'s proposed rate of 3.25% of Net Room Revenue falls below the 25th percentile and places the proposed transaction in the bottom decile of the data set when adjusted for portfolio size and brand strength.

If the Veltris IP Licensing team and Brand Governance Committee determine that any concession below the 4.0% policy floor is warranted to secure the Peregrine transaction, Whitfield Barr recommends that such concession be accompanied by structural protections designed to limit the long-term revenue impact, including but not limited to:

> \(a\) An enhanced Minimum Annual Guarantee set at no less than 85% of projected Year 1 royalties calculated at the 4.0% rate, to ensure a floor of approximately \$2,652,000 per year regardless of the negotiated percentage rate;
>
> \(b\) A royalty step-up schedule, under which the negotiated rate increases by specified increments (e.g., 25 basis points per year) over the initial term until it reaches the 4.0% policy floor or a mutually agreed target rate;
>
> \(c\) A most-favored-licensee provision, under which Veltris retains the right to adjust the Peregrine royalty rate upward if a subsequent AURANOVA licensee is granted a higher rate for a comparable transaction.

**B. Quality Control and Enforcement Protections**

Based on the enforcement risk analysis set forth in Part IV of this memorandum, Whitfield Barr concludes that the three proposed quality control modifications --- reduced audit frequency, deemed-approval mechanisms, and affiliate sublicensing without consent --- create individually material and cumulatively severe enforcement risks. These risks include naked licensing exposure, trademark dilution, and loss-of-rights scenarios under Lanham Act § 45 (15 U.S.C. § 1127), as well as the weakening of Veltris\'s ability to assert infringement and dilution claims with respect to the AURANOVA Marks.

Whitfield Barr\'s specific recommendations are as follows:

> \(a\) **Deemed-Approval Clauses: Reject Entirely.** Deemed-approval clauses should be rejected in their entirety as inconsistent with Veltris\'s obligations as trademark owner and as creating an unacceptable litigation risk to the AURANOVA registrations. No modification or mitigation of this provision --- such as extending the deemed-approval period from fifteen to thirty days --- adequately addresses the fundamental structural problem. The risk is inherent in the mechanism itself, not in the length of the review period.
>
> \(b\) **Audit Frequency: Maintain Semi-Annual Minimum.** On-site quality audit frequency should remain semi-annual at minimum, and the notice requirement should not exceed ten business days. If Peregrine objects to the frequency or notice requirements, an alternative structure --- such as unannounced \"spot check\" audits in addition to scheduled semi-annual reviews --- may be offered as a compromise, provided that the net effect is to increase rather than decrease the overall level of licensor oversight.
>
> \(c\) **Affiliate Sublicensing: Condition on Safeguards.** If any flexibility on affiliate sublicensing is considered, it should be subject to the minimum safeguards outlined in Section IV.D of this memorandum, including advance identification of each affiliate, execution of direct quality control undertakings, independent audit rights, and an immediate cessation right. No blanket authorization for affiliate sublicensing should be granted.

IP Licensing team in connection with the internal escalation of the Peregrine Hospitality Group, LLC trademark license negotiation under Veltris IP Licensing Policy § 6. **[MEMORANDUM]{.underline}**

**TO:** Jason Murata, Vice President, IP Licensing, Veltris Consumer Brands, Inc.

**CC:** David Feingold, Associate Counsel, IP Licensing

**FROM:** Claire Okonkwo, Senior Counsel, IP Licensing

**DATE:** March 15, 2025

**RE:** AURANOVA / Peregrine Hospitality Group --- Negotiation History and Redline Summary (IPL-2025-0019)

**CONFIDENTIAL --- ATTORNEY WORK PRODUCT / ATTORNEY-CLIENT PRIVILEGED**

This memorandum has been prepared by counsel at the direction of and for the benefit of Veltris Consumer Brands, Inc. and is protected by the attorney-client privilege and the attorney work-product doctrine. This memorandum and the information contained herein are strictly confidential and may not be disclosed, distributed, or copied, in whole or in part, without the prior written consent of the Legal Department of Veltris Consumer Brands, Inc.

**[I. Purpose]{.underline}**

This memorandum provides a comprehensive chronological summary of the trademark license negotiation between Veltris Consumer Brands, Inc. (\"Veltris\" or the \"Company\") and Peregrine Hospitality Group, LLC (\"Peregrine\") for the co-branded \"AURANOVA by Peregrine\" boutique hotel concept. The memorandum covers the full negotiation period from Peregrine\'s initial inbound licensing inquiry on September 3, 2024 through receipt of Peregrine\'s fourth redline of the Trademark License Agreement (the \"TLA\") on March 14, 2025. It catalogs each substantive exchange between the parties, identifies the current state of play on all material terms, and maps each disputed provision against the applicable delegated authority thresholds set forth in the Veltris IP Licensing Policy.

This memorandum has been prepared to serve as the factual background and predicate document for the forthcoming escalation memorandum to the Chief Legal Officer and Chief Financial Officer, as well as the Brand Governance Committee. The escalation memorandum, which is being prepared separately, will incorporate specific recommendations regarding potential concessions and approval requests. The present memorandum is limited to factual and procedural history and does not contain negotiation strategy recommendations.

This memorandum should be read alongside the Veltris IP Licensing Policy, Rev. 4.0 (effective April 12, 2024), particularly §§ 5.1--5.8 (setting forth approved commercial terms, quality control standards, termination parameters, sublicensing requirements, and governing law defaults) and § 6 (establishing the delegated authority framework and escalation procedures for out-of-policy deviations). All references to \"policy\" or \"IP Licensing Policy\" in this memorandum are to that document unless otherwise specified.

**[II. Transaction Overview]{.underline}**

Peregrine Hospitality Group, LLC is a privately held hospitality company headquartered in Atlanta, Georgia. Peregrine operates a portfolio of 34 boutique hotels concentrated across the southeastern United States. The company\'s properties are positioned in the upper-midscale to upscale segments, targeting leisure and business travelers in urban and resort-adjacent markets. Peregrine\'s portfolio is managed through a series of affiliated property management entities, several of which are majority-owned subsidiaries and others of which are structured as joint ventures with local ownership groups.

The proposed transaction contemplates a trademark license pursuant to which Peregrine would rebrand 12 of its existing boutique hotel properties under the \"AURANOVA by Peregrine\" co-branded mark. The 12 target properties are distributed across the licensed territory of six southeastern states: Georgia, Florida, South Carolina, North Carolina, Tennessee, and Alabama. The licensed marks are AURANOVA U.S. Trademark Registration Nos. 5,417,832; 5,822,109; and 6,004,561, all of which are owned by Veltris Consumer Brands, Inc. and are currently in active use in connection with the Company\'s premium consumer lifestyle branding portfolio.

Peregrine\'s target launch date for the first three \"AURANOVA by Peregrine\" properties --- located in Savannah, Georgia; Charleston, South Carolina; and Nashville, Tennessee --- is June 1, 2025. The remaining nine properties are planned for phased rollout over the subsequent 18 months, with completion of full portfolio rebranding projected for December 2026.

Peregrine\'s outside counsel for this transaction is Diane Sheehan, Partner, at Calloway, Sheehan & Pratt LLP, Atlanta, Georgia. Ms. Sheehan has represented Peregrine across multiple prior licensing and franchise transactions and has been the primary drafting counterpart on the Peregrine side throughout the TLA negotiation. Veltris\'s external IP licensing advisor for this transaction is Robert Whitfield, Partner, at Whitfield Barr LLP, Charlotte, North Carolina. Mr. Whitfield has provided drafting support, IP valuation benchmarking, and enforcement risk analysis throughout the negotiation process.

The parties entered into a Mutual Non-Disclosure Agreement dated November 18, 2024 (Veltris Ref. No. NDA-2024-0347), which governs the confidential treatment of all financial, commercial, and proprietary information exchanged between the parties in connection with this transaction. All financial projections, draft agreements, redlines, and correspondence referenced herein have been exchanged under the protections of that NDA.

**[III. Chronological Negotiation History]{.underline}**

**A. Initial Inbound Inquiry --- September 3, 2024**

On September 3, 2024, the IP Licensing team received an inbound inquiry from Marcus Healy, Vice President of Development at Peregrine Hospitality Group, LLC. The inquiry was transmitted via email to the general IP licensing inbox and was routed to the IP Licensing team on September 4, 2024. In the inquiry, Mr. Healy expressed Peregrine\'s interest in exploring a co-branded boutique hotel licensing arrangement leveraging the AURANOVA brand. The inquiry described Peregrine\'s southeastern footprint in general terms and referenced Peregrine\'s view that the AURANOVA brand\'s positioning in the premium consumer lifestyle space would be complementary to Peregrine\'s existing guest demographic and property profile.

Upon receipt, the IP Licensing team conducted a preliminary assessment of brand fit and strategic alignment. This assessment included a review of Peregrine\'s publicly available property portfolio, financial standing (based on publicly available information at that time), and market positioning. The team confirmed that Peregrine\'s 34-property portfolio and its concentration in the southeastern United States fell within the regional parameters established by the IP Licensing Policy for hospitality-sector trademark licenses. No disqualifying brand conflicts or reputational concerns were identified during this preliminary review.

The inquiry was formally logged as IPL-2025-0019 on September 10, 2024, and internal routing was completed to assign the matter to the IP Licensing team, with Claire Okonkwo designated as lead negotiating counsel and David Feingold as supporting associate counsel. Jason Murata, VP, IP Licensing, was briefed on the matter on September 12, 2024, and authorized the team to proceed with preliminary discussions.

**B. Preliminary Discussions and NDA --- September--November 2024**

Between mid-September and mid-November 2024, Claire Okonkwo and Diane Sheehan of Calloway, Sheehan & Pratt LLP conducted a series of introductory telephone calls and video conferences to establish the commercial parameters of the proposed transaction. These discussions covered Peregrine\'s interest in the AURANOVA brand, the scope of the proposed licensed territory, the number and identity of the target properties, Peregrine\'s general timeline for rebranding, and the high-level commercial structure of the anticipated license arrangement. During this period, the parties also exchanged general background information regarding their respective organizations, licensing philosophies, and transaction processes.

In parallel, the parties negotiated the terms of a Mutual Non-Disclosure Agreement to facilitate the exchange of confidential financial and business information. Following approximately three weeks of negotiation --- principally involving the scope of permitted disclosures, the term of confidentiality obligations, and the carve-outs for legally compelled disclosure --- the Mutual NDA was executed on November 18, 2024 and assigned Veltris Ref. No. NDA-2024-0347. The NDA has a two-year term with a five-year survival period for trade secret and proprietary information.

Following execution of the NDA, Peregrine provided preliminary financial information regarding the 12 target properties, including projected Net Room Revenue for Year 1 of the proposed license term. Peregrine\'s financial projections, which are set forth in detail in Attachment I (Exhibit D to the Term Sheet), estimated aggregate Year 1 Net Room Revenue for the 12 target properties at approximately \$78,000,000. These projections were prepared by Peregrine\'s internal finance team and were provided subject to the confidentiality protections of NDA-2024-0347. The Veltris IP Licensing team reviewed these projections and shared them with Robert Whitfield at Whitfield Barr LLP for purposes of IP valuation benchmarking and comparable transaction analysis.

**C. First Term Sheet --- January 6, 2025**

On January 6, 2025, Veltris issued the first formal term sheet to Peregrine, setting forth the Company\'s proposed commercial terms for the trademark license. The term sheet was prepared by the IP Licensing team with input from Robert Whitfield at Whitfield Barr LLP and was reviewed and approved by Jason Murata prior to issuance. All terms proposed in the initial term sheet were within the parameters established by the IP Licensing Policy, Rev. 4.0. The key commercial terms as proposed were as follows:

> • **Royalty Rate:** 4.0% of Net Room Revenue, which represents the policy floor rate for hospitality-sector trademark licenses as set forth in § 5.2(a) of the IP Licensing Policy.
>
> • **Minimum Annual Guarantee (MAG):** \$2,340,000, calculated as 75% of the projected Year 1 royalty at the floor rate (i.e., 75% × 4.0% × \$78,000,000 = \$2,340,000), consistent with the minimum MAG threshold prescribed by § 5.2(b) of the IP Licensing Policy.
>
> • **Upfront License Fee:** \$750,000, payable upon execution of the TLA. This amount exceeds the policy minimum of \$500,000 established for hospitality-sector trademark licenses and was set at this level based on the scope of the licensed territory and the number of target properties.
>
> • **Initial Term:** 7 years, with mutual renewal options. The 7-year initial term represents the maximum initial term permitted under § 5.1(a) of the IP Licensing Policy. Renewal options were proposed as mutual (i.e., requiring both parties\' consent), consistent with the policy default.
>
> • **Quality Control:** Semi-annual on-site audits of licensed properties, on 5 business days\' advance written notice to the licensee, consistent with § 5.3 of the IP Licensing Policy.
>
> • **Licensor Convenience Termination:** Veltris to have the right to terminate the TLA for convenience upon 180 days\' prior written notice, exercisable after the third anniversary of the effective date, consistent with § 5.5(a) of the IP Licensing Policy.
>
> • **Post-Termination Sell-Off Period:** 12 months following the effective date of termination or expiration, representing the maximum sell-off period permitted under § 5.5(c) of the IP Licensing Policy.
>
> • **Sublicensing:** Prior written consent of Veltris required for all sublicenses, with no exceptions, consistent with § 5.6 of the IP Licensing Policy.
>
> • **Indemnification and Liability Caps:** Uncapped licensee indemnification of the licensor for all claims arising from the licensee\'s use of the licensed marks. Licensor\'s aggregate liability capped at the trailing 12-month royalties actually paid, consistent with § 5.4 of the IP Licensing Policy.
>
> • **Governing Law and Dispute Resolution:** North Carolina law, with exclusive jurisdiction in the state courts of Mecklenburg County, North Carolina, consistent with the policy default under § 5.7. No arbitration provision.
>
> • **Deemed Approval:** None. The term sheet expressly provided that no approval or consent of the licensor shall be deemed granted by reason of the licensor\'s failure to respond within any specified period, consistent with the prohibition on deemed approval mechanisms set forth in § 5.3(c) of the IP Licensing Policy.

Peregrine acknowledged receipt of the term sheet on January 9, 2025. In its acknowledgment, Peregrine indicated general commercial interest in the proposed transaction and expressed alignment with the overall structure of the co-branded concept. However, Peregrine flagged several terms as requiring internal review with its board of directors and outside counsel, specifically identifying the royalty rate, term length, audit provisions, termination mechanics, sublicensing restrictions, indemnification structure, and governing law/dispute resolution as areas of anticipated discussion.

**D. First Draft TLA --- February 2025**

In early February 2025, Veltris circulated the first full-form draft of the Trademark License Agreement to Peregrine. The draft TLA was prepared by the IP Licensing team with substantial drafting input from Robert Whitfield at Whitfield Barr LLP and reflected all of the commercial positions set forth in the January 6, 2025 term sheet. The draft was a comprehensive, 47-page agreement organized into 22 articles, together with exhibits covering brand usage guidelines, property specifications, licensed marks and registrations, reporting templates, and insurance requirements.

Peregrine\'s outside counsel, Diane Sheehan, provided an initial written response to the draft TLA on February 14, 2025, in the form of a detailed comment letter. In that letter, Ms. Sheehan acknowledged substantive alignment between the parties on the following terms: the licensed territory (Georgia, Florida, South Carolina, North Carolina, Tennessee, and Alabama), the upfront license fee (\$750,000), the brand usage guidelines framework (subject to minor conforming edits), and the general structure of the quality standards provisions. However, Ms. Sheehan previewed substantive concerns and indicated that Peregrine would be submitting a marked redline addressing the royalty rate, term length and renewal structure, audit provisions, termination mechanics, sublicensing restrictions, indemnification and liability cap structure, and governing law/dispute resolution. That redline was received on February 21, 2025, as discussed immediately below.

**E. Peregrine\'s First Redline**

On February 21, 2025, Peregrine transmitted its first redline of the draft TLA. The redline was prepared by Diane Sheehan of Calloway, Sheehan & Pratt LLP and was accompanied by a detailed cover letter explaining Peregrine\'s positions on each disputed term. The key movements and positions reflected in the first redline were as follows:

**Royalty Rate.** Peregrine proposed reducing the royalty rate from 4.0% to 2.75% of Net Room Revenue. Peregrine\'s stated rationale, as set forth in Ms. Sheehan\'s cover letter, was that Peregrine\'s significant capital expenditure commitment for property rebranding --- estimated at approximately \$4.2 million across the 12 target properties --- justifies a substantially lower royalty rate to ensure commercially viable returns on its rebranding investment. Peregrine characterized the 2.75% rate as consistent with comparable co-branded hospitality licenses in the southeastern United States. Veltris\'s response held firm at 4.0%, which represents the policy floor under § 5.2(a), and communicated that any rate below 4.0% would be outside the IP Licensing team\'s delegated authority.

**Term.** Peregrine proposed extending the initial term from 7 years to 10 years and adding two 5-year unilateral (licensee-only) renewal options, for a potential total term of 20 years. Peregrine\'s stated rationale was that its capital expenditure payback period for the \$4.2 million rebranding investment substantially exceeds 7 years, and that Peregrine requires certainty of continued brand access over a longer horizon to justify the investment. Veltris maintained its position of a 7-year initial term with mutual-only renewal options, consistent with the policy maximum under § 5.1(a).

**Minimum Annual Guarantee.** Peregrine proposed reducing the MAG from \$2,340,000 to \$1,500,000. Peregrine stated that the higher MAG failed to account for the ramp-up risk inherent in newly branded properties and argued that the MAG should reflect realistic Year 1 occupancy rates rather than optimistic projections. Veltris maintained the \$2,340,000 MAG, calculated in accordance with the policy threshold methodology.

**Audit Frequency and Notice.** Peregrine proposed reducing audit frequency from semi-annual to annual on-site audits and extending the notice period from 5 business days to 30 business days. Peregrine\'s stated rationale was that semi-annual on-site audits with short notice periods would cause significant operational disruption to hotel operations and could negatively impact the guest experience, particularly during peak occupancy seasons. Veltris maintained its policy position of semi-annual audits on 5 business days\' notice.

**Sublicensing.** Peregrine proposed that sublicensing to \"controlled affiliates,\" defined as entities in which Peregrine holds greater than 50% direct or indirect ownership, should be permitted without prior Veltris consent. Peregrine stated that this flexibility was essential given its operational structure, which relies on affiliated property management entities to manage day-to-day hotel operations, and that requiring prior consent for routine intra-group sublicenses would create unacceptable delays in property management decisions. Veltris maintained its policy position requiring prior written consent for all sublicenses, without exception.

**Deemed Approval.** Peregrine introduced a new deemed approval provision under which Veltris\'s approval of marketing materials and certain brand usage submissions would be deemed granted automatically if Veltris failed to respond within 10 business days of submission. Peregrine stated that this provision was necessary for speed-to-market for seasonal marketing campaigns and property launch materials. Veltris rejected the deemed approval provision in its entirety, consistent with the express prohibition on deemed approval mechanisms under § 5.3(c) of the IP Licensing Policy.

**Termination.** Peregrine proposed eliminating the licensor\'s convenience termination right entirely and replacing it with breach-only termination, with a 120-day cure period for any breach by the licensee. Peregrine further proposed extending the post-termination sell-off period from 12 months to 24 months. Peregrine\'s stated rationale for eliminating convenience termination was that its substantial capital expenditure investment requires certainty of continued rights and that a unilateral exit right for the licensor would undermine Peregrine\'s ability to justify the rebranding investment to its board and lenders. The extended sell-off was justified on the basis that the hospitality industry requires a longer wind-down period to accommodate existing reservations, loyalty program transitions, and the orderly removal of co-branded signage and materials. Veltris maintained its policy positions on all termination-related provisions.

**Indemnification and Liability Caps.** Peregrine proposed capping its licensee indemnification obligation at 1× annual royalties (based on the preceding 12-month period) and increasing the licensor\'s aggregate liability cap from trailing 12-month royalties to total royalties paid over the full term of the agreement. Peregrine cited proportionality concerns and corporate governance limitations on uncapped contractual exposure as the basis for these positions. Veltris maintained its policy positions of uncapped licensee indemnification and a trailing 12-month licensor liability cap.

**Governing Law and Dispute Resolution.** Peregrine proposed replacing North Carolina governing law with Georgia law and substituting AAA arbitration in Atlanta, Georgia for litigation in Mecklenburg County, North Carolina. Peregrine stated that, as a Georgia-headquartered entity, its principal jurisdiction should govern the agreement and that arbitration is the more appropriate dispute resolution mechanism for commercial licensing disputes in the hospitality sector. Veltris maintained its policy default of North Carolina law and Mecklenburg County state courts.

**Areas of Agreement.** Notwithstanding the foregoing disputes, the first redline confirmed alignment between the parties on the following terms: licensed territory, upfront license fee amount (\$750,000), brand usage guidelines framework (subject to minor conforming language), insurance requirements (including minimum coverage levels and additional insured endorsements), and the general structure of the reporting and record-keeping obligations.

The IP Licensing team reviewed Peregrine\'s first redline and prepared a detailed written response, which was transmitted to Diane Sheehan on February 27, 2025. The response communicated Veltris\'s position on each disputed term and indicated that multiple of Peregrine\'s positions fell outside the IP Licensing team\'s delegated authority.

**F. Peregrine\'s Second Redline**

Peregrine transmitted its second redline on March 3, 2025. The second redline reflected incremental movement on several disputed terms, though the magnitude of movement remained modest relative to the gaps between the parties. The key changes from the first to the second redline were as follows:

**Royalty Rate.** Peregrine moved its proposed royalty rate from 2.75% to 3.0% of Net Room Revenue, representing an upward adjustment of 25 basis points. Veltris continued to hold at the 4.0% policy floor rate.

**Minimum Annual Guarantee.** Peregrine moved its proposed MAG from \$1,500,000 to \$1,650,000, an increase of \$150,000. Veltris continued to hold at \$2,340,000.

**Audit Notice Period.** Peregrine adjusted its proposed audit notice period from 30 business days to 25 business days but maintained its position that audits should be conducted on an annual rather than semi-annual basis. Veltris continued to hold the policy position of semi-annual audits on 5 business days\' notice.

**Termination Cure Period.** Peregrine reduced its proposed cure period for licensee breaches from 120 days to 90 days. Peregrine maintained its positions that licensor convenience termination should be eliminated entirely and that the post-termination sell-off period should be 24 months.

**Deemed Approval.** Peregrine adjusted its proposed deemed approval trigger period from 10 business days to 15 business days of non-response, but continued to insist on the inclusion of an automatic approval mechanism. Veltris continued to reject any form of deemed approval, consistent with the express prohibition in § 5.3(c) of the IP Licensing Policy.

All other disputed positions --- including the 10-year initial term, unilateral licensee renewal options, sublicensing without consent to controlled affiliates, capped licensee indemnity at 1× annual royalties, licensor liability cap at total term royalties, Georgia governing law, and AAA arbitration in Atlanta --- remained unchanged from Peregrine\'s first redline.

In its written response to the second redline, transmitted on March 6, 2025, the Veltris IP Licensing team reiterated its positions on all disputed terms and communicated clearly that multiple positions remained outside the team\'s delegated authority under the IP Licensing Policy. The team expressly advised Peregrine\'s counsel that further concessions on several terms would require formal escalation to senior leadership within Veltris, including the Chief Legal Officer and Chief Financial Officer.

**G. Peregrine\'s Third Redline**

Peregrine transmitted its third redline on March 10, 2025. This redline reflected further movement on certain key commercial terms and introduced new qualifications on others. The key changes were as follows:

**Royalty Rate.** Peregrine moved its proposed royalty rate from 3.0% to 3.25% of Net Room Revenue, representing an additional upward adjustment of 25 basis points. In her cover correspondence, Diane Sheehan stated that 3.25% represented Peregrine\'s \"best and final\" position on the royalty rate, reflecting the maximum degree of flexibility that Peregrine\'s board of directors was prepared to approve given the magnitude of Peregrine\'s capital expenditure commitment for property rebranding.

**Minimum Annual Guarantee.** Peregrine moved its proposed MAG from \$1,650,000 to \$1,800,000, an increase of \$150,000. Ms. Sheehan\'s cover correspondence stated that \$1,800,000 represented Peregrine\'s final position on the MAG.

**Upfront License Fee.** The upfront license fee remained at \$750,000, which has been an agreed term since the term sheet stage.

**Term and Renewal.** Peregrine continued to propose a 10-year initial term with two 5-year unilateral (licensee-only) renewal options. However, Peregrine conceded for the first time that the renewal options could be made subject to a \"market-rate adjustment mechanism\" pursuant to which the royalty rate applicable during each renewal period would be subject to adjustment to reflect then-prevailing market rates for comparable hospitality trademark licenses. The specific mechanics of the adjustment mechanism were not fully developed in the third redline, and Peregrine indicated its willingness to negotiate the details of this provision.

**[VII. Peregrine\'s Movement Across Redlines --- Trajectory Summary]{.underline}**

To assist in evaluating Peregrine\'s negotiating posture and the likelihood of further concessions, the following narrative tracks the directional movement of Peregrine\'s positions across the four redlines received to date. This trajectory analysis illustrates the pace and pattern of Peregrine\'s concessions and identifies the point at which movement ceased on each term.

**Royalty Rate.** Peregrine\'s opening position was 2.75% of Net Room Revenue (first redline). This was adjusted to 3.0% in the second redline, and further to 3.25% in the third redline, where Peregrine characterized the rate as its \"best and final\" position. The fourth redline confirmed no further movement. Total movement toward Veltris: 50 basis points across three redlines, representing approximately 40% of the gap between Peregrine\'s opening position and the Veltris policy floor. The remaining gap is 75 basis points.

**Minimum Annual Guarantee.** Peregrine\'s opening position was \$1,500,000 (first redline). This was adjusted to \$1,650,000 in the second redline and to \$1,800,000 in the third redline, which Peregrine characterized as its final position. The fourth redline confirmed no further movement. Total movement toward Veltris: \$300,000 across three redlines, representing approximately 36% of the gap between Peregrine\'s opening position and the Veltris policy threshold. The remaining gap is \$540,000.

**Audit Notice Period.** Peregrine\'s opening position was 30 business days (first redline). This was adjusted to 25 business days in the second redline and to 20 business days in the third redline. The fourth redline confirmed no further movement. Movement has been in the direction of the Veltris position, but a substantial gap remains (20 days versus 5 days). Peregrine has maintained its position on annual (rather than semi-annual) audit frequency throughout all four redlines.

**Termination Cure Period.** Peregrine\'s opening position was a 120-day cure period (first redline). This was reduced to 90 days in the second redline. No further movement was made in the third or fourth redlines. Peregrine has maintained its positions on the elimination of licensor convenience termination and a 24-month post-termination sell-off throughout all four redlines without any movement.

**Deemed Approval.** Peregrine\'s opening position was automatic approval after 10 business days of non-response (first redline). This was adjusted to 15 business days in the second redline. No further movement was made in the third or fourth redlines. This provision remains a binary dispute --- Veltris\'s policy prohibits any form of deemed approval, while Peregrine insists on some mechanism.

**Licensee Indemnity Cap.** Peregrine\'s opening position was a cap of 1× annual royalties (first redline). This was adjusted to 2× Year 1 annual royalties in the third redline. No further movement was made in the fourth redline. The licensee indemnity remains capped in Peregrine\'s proposal, whereas Veltris\'s policy requires uncapped indemnification.

**All Other Disputed Terms.** Peregrine has made no movement from its initial positions on the following terms across any of the four redlines: 10-year initial term, unilateral licensee renewal options, sublicensing to controlled affiliates without consent, elimination of licensor convenience termination, 24-month post-termination sell-off, licensor liability cap at total term royalties, Georgia governing law, and AAA arbitration in Atlanta.

In summary, Peregrine\'s movement has effectively plateaued as of the third redline. The fourth redline confirms that Peregrine treats its current positions as final across all disputed terms. This plateau, combined with Peregrine\'s communication of an April 15, 2025 board-approval deadline, indicates that any further movement will require concessions from the Veltris side or a mutual compromise framework developed at the escalation level.
